claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
subclaims: Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities?
Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?
Is the limitation of parameter-based knowledge editing geometric rather than incidental?
Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?
Do localized weight edits propagate globally?
Does damage compound as edits accumulate?
Does a parameter-free approach leave the model weights untouched?
Is a parameter-free approach a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback?

experiments: To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a standardized large-scale benchmark comparing parameter-based editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained FT) against a parameter-free method such as IKE or SERAC-style retrieval/edit memories on the same base models (e.g., GPT-J 6B and LLaMA-2-7B) using publicly available datasets COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, RippleEdits, MQuAKE-CF, MQuAKE-T, and COUNTERFACT+ from HuggingFace/EasyEdit. Use the realistic protocols already suggested by the evidence: filter to facts the base model originally recalls, evaluate not only efficacy/generalization/locality on standard prompts but also dynamic neighborhood prompts, ripple-aware related-fact tests, portability tests, multi-hop questions, and broad post-edit capability checks on public benchmarks like HellaSwag, MMLU, LAMBADA, TriviaQA, and perplexity on Wikipedia. Include both single-edit and sequential/batch-edit settings with edit counts such as 1, 10, 100, 1000, and report confidence intervals. If prior near-perfect results survive all these harder evaluations while preserving downstream capability scores, that weakens the claim. If apparent success on standard edit prompts collapses under ripple, portability, multi-hop, or capability evaluations, that supports the claim that prior reports were overly optimistic and that parameter-free approaches are credible alternatives. This experiment becomes less necessary if there already exists a fully standardized public leaderboard with all methods re-run under these exact realistic protocols and common implementations.

To address subclaim 5 and subclaim 6, perform a sequential edit stress test focused on whether damage propagates globally and compounds as edits accumulate. Starting from an unedited model, apply edits one at a time using parameter-based methods and, separately, a parameter-free baseline that leaves weights unchanged. After each edit or small block of edits, measure: (i) success on the edited fact, (ii) specificity/locality on held-out unrelated prompts from COUNTERFACT+ and RippleEdits neighborhoods, (iii) hidden-state drift and output KL divergence on a large unrelated corpus such as Wikipedia or Natural Questions, and (iv) general task performance on fixed public slices of HellaSwag, MMLU, and LAMBADA. Also test geographic spread inside the model by logging per-layer activation and logit changes for unrelated prompts before vs after edits. If unrelated outputs and hidden states drift progressively with edit count, and task scores degrade monotonically or superlinearly for parameter edits but not for the parameter-free method, that supports global propagation and compounding damage. If drift remains tightly localized and capability metrics stay flat even after many edits, that argues against those subclaims. This experiment could be partly superseded by stronger existing evidence if prior work already released full per-edit trajectories, unrelated-corpus KL measurements, and downstream capability curves across long edit sequences.

To address subclaim 3 and subclaim 4, test the proposed geometric mechanism directly by relating each localized weight edit to the representation covariance structure of the model. For a base model such as GPT-J or LLaMA-2-7B, collect hidden representations for large public corpora (Wikipedia, Natural Questions, or C4 subsets from HuggingFace) at the layers where edits are applied, estimate the covariance eigenspectrum, and decompose each edit-induced activation change or effective weight-update action into principal directions. Then quantify whether edit effects are disproportionately aligned with low-variance directions and whether alignment predicts downstream collateral damage: for each edit, compute projection mass onto low- vs high-variance eigenspaces, resulting changes in target token logits, neighborhood KL, locality failures, and broader capability degradation. A stronger causal version is to construct matched synthetic perturbations of equal norm injected along low-variance and high-variance directions and compare how much they alter unrelated outputs globally. If low-variance alignment consistently predicts larger nonlocal behavioral changes and synthetic low-variance perturbations cause more widespread disruption, that supports a geometric rather than incidental limitation. If edit harm is uncorrelated with covariance geometry, or high-variance directions are equally or more damaging, the geometric account is weakened. This experiment could become less necessary if prior mechanistic studies already provide public, reproducible eigenspace analyses linking edit amplification to collateral damage across multiple models and editing methods.

To address subclaim 1, run a realistic head-to-head evaluation of parameter-based editors versus a parameter-free baseline. Use public datasets COUNTERFACT/COUNTERFACT+, ZSRE, RippleEdits, MQuAKE, Natural Questions, plus general-capability benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and GSM8K. On an open model such as GPT-J-6B or Llama-2-7B, compare ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and a parameter-free in-context or retrieval-based editing method such as IKE/RAG-style prompting. Evaluate not only single-prompt edit success, but paraphrase generalization, dynamic neighborhood locality, portability, multi-hop consistency, perplexity, and downstream task degradation before and after editing. Also verify the parameter-free method by hashing or checksuming model weights before and after use. If parameter editors retain high efficacy while preserving locality, perplexity, and general benchmark scores under this broader protocol, the claim that they cannot reliably update knowledge without damage is weakened. If their near-perfect edit scores collapse under paraphrases, dynamic neighborhoods, multi-hop tests, or general-capability checks while the parameter-free method is competitive, the claim is supported. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by a large, independently replicated benchmark already reporting these exact metrics, confidence intervals, and unchanged-weight verification for parameter-free methods.

To address subclaim 6, perform a sequential and batch edit scaling study to test whether damage compounds as edits accumulate. Starting from the same base model and using recallable facts from COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and MQuAKE-CF, apply edit counts k = 1, 10, 100, 1000, and, if feasible, 3000 with ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning; include the best-performing parameter-free method from Experiment 1 as a non-weight-changing comparator. After each edit block, remeasure edit efficacy, paraphrase success, locality on unrelated and semantically adjacent facts, RippleEdits consistency, MQuAKE multi-hop accuracy, held-out Natural Questions accuracy, LAMBADA/WikiText perplexity, and MMLU/HellaSwag scores. Track whether earlier edits are forgotten and whether unrelated predictions drift. If degradation grows approximately monotonically or superlinearly with edit count, especially while individual edit success remains high, this supports the claim that damage compounds globally. If many edits can be accumulated with stable locality and stable general capability, the compounding-damage subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be avoided only if prior work already provided open logs for large-k sequential and batch editing with the same broad capability and locality measurements, not just edit-success scores.

To address subclaim 4, test the proposed geometric mechanism directly by measuring whether localized weight edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions. For the layers targeted by ROME/MEMIT or other editors, estimate the hidden-state covariance spectrum using public text such as WikiText-103, Wikipedia, or The Pile subsets available on HuggingFace. For each factual edit from COUNTERFACT or ZSRE, decompose the induced activation change and weight-update effect into the covariance eigenbasis, then measure amplification as a function of eigenvalue size and correlate it with downstream logit shifts on unrelated prompts, locality failures, and benchmark degradation. Include controls such as random low-norm updates matched in Frobenius norm, edits constrained away from low-variance directions, and edits projected onto high-variance directions. If harmful global logit shifts and locality failures are concentrated in low-variance eigendirections, and suppressing those components reduces damage while preserving edit success, the geometric subclaim is supported. If amplification is not related to representation variance, or if low-variance projections do not predict damage, the limitation looks less geometric and more method-specific or incidental. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released mechanistic analyses that already publish layerwise covariance spectra, edit decompositions, and causal tests linking low-variance directions to post-edit failures.

To address subclaim 2 ('Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?'), first reproduce the standard published evaluation and then run a preregistered stress test on two open-weight models, such as GPT-J-6B and Llama-3.1-8B, using standardized EasyEdit implementations of ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit, constrained fine-tuning, and an unedited control. Draw edits from the publicly available COUNTERFACT and ZSRE datasets, retaining only facts the base model recalls, and evaluate on held-out paraphrases, COUNTERFACT+ dynamic neighborhoods, RippleEdits related facts, and MQuAKE multi-hop questions. Measure efficacy, paraphrase generalization, portability, neighborhood KL divergence, unrelated-fact accuracy, and pre/post performance on public MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, LAMBADA, and WikiText-103 perplexity. Compare these methods with parameter-free in-context editing and retrieval from the same edit records, controlling the amount of evidence shown and reporting paired bootstrap confidence intervals and preregistered non-inferiority margins. If parameter methods retain high edit success without significant locality or capability loss, the broad claim is weakened for the tested models and edit regime; if standard scores remain near-perfect but fall sharply under dynamic neighborhoods, multi-hop tests, or general benchmarks, this supports the assertion that prior evaluation was unrealistic. If the parameter-free systems match editing accuracy and preserve capabilities at acceptable latency and memory cost, they qualify as serious alternatives rather than merely fallbacks. This experiment could be made largely unnecessary by public checkpoints, exact prompts, and complete per-example pre/post outputs from prior studies covering all of these stress tests and controls.

To address subclaim 4 ('Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?'), instrument the most informative parameter-editing methods from Experiment 1. For each edited layer, estimate the covariance eigenspectrum of its input representations using a public WikiText-103 sample, then decompose the actual weight update into covariance-eigenvector bins. Quantify update gain in each bin, for example ||ΔWv_i|| relative to the eigenvalue λ_i and to the corresponding baseline transformation ||Wv_i||, and trace resulting activation differences through all later layers and output KL divergence on unrelated WikiText-103, COUNTERFACT neighborhood, and Natural Questions prompts. Test causality rather than correlation by constructing matched-efficacy controls: re-optimize edits while suppressing low-variance components, align otherwise comparable updates with high-variance components, and use norm-matched random rotations, all while holding the target-fact logit change approximately constant. Repeat across models, methods, layers, and seeds. A consistent inverse relationship between representation variance and normalized gain, together with reduced global KL or benchmark damage when low-variance components are suppressed, would support the geometric mechanism and help explain global propagation; no relationship, or equal damage from matched high-variance and random controls, would favor an incidental implementation-specific explanation. Layerwise activation changes confined to prompts related to the edited fact would also contradict the global-propagation subclaim, whereas broad changes on unrelated prompts would support it. This experiment could be avoided if prior work released weight deltas, representative activation covariances, and matched-efficacy directional-ablation results sufficient to reproduce these analyses.

To address subclaim 6 ('Does damage compound as edits accumulate?'), use the best-performing parameter method and parameter-free baseline identified in Experiment 1 and apply conflict-filtered edits from public COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and MQuAKE-CF at cumulative counts of 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and, where feasible, 3,000. Run both sequential and same-size batch editing from the identical base checkpoint, randomize edit order over multiple seeds, and evaluate after every logarithmically spaced checkpoint. Track retained success on all earlier edits, paraphrase and multi-hop accuracy, unrelated-fact locality, output KL, WikiText-103 perplexity, and MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and LAMBADA performance. Fit dose-response models that distinguish constant, linear, and superlinear degradation, and test whether the geometric low-variance score measured in Experiment 2 predicts which runs deteriorate fastest. For the parameter-free system, store edits externally, verify bitwise hashes of every model tensor before and after evaluation, and report retrieval accuracy, context-window failures, latency, and memory growth as well as task quality. Monotonic loss of old edits or core capabilities, especially superlinear loss associated with low-variance update energy, would support cumulative geometric damage; flat capability curves with sustained edit retention would refute it over the tested range. Matching quality with unchanged weight hashes and manageable resource costs would support both the weight-untouched and serious-alternative subclaims, whereas poor retrieval, excessive cost, or weak reasoning would limit that conclusion. Public sequential-edit checkpoints and complete metric trajectories across these edit counts could make rerunning this experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaim 1 and subclaim 2, run a head-to-head benchmark of parameter-based knowledge editing methods under realistic post-edit evaluation. Use a public autoregressive model such as Llama-2-7B or Mistral-7B, and implement representative parameter-editing methods from prior work (for example ROME, MEMIT, MEND) using standard public edit benchmarks such as CounterFact and zsRE from HuggingFace or the original public releases. For each requested fact edit, evaluate not just immediate rewrite success but also paraphrase generalization, neighborhood specificity, multi-hop consistency, resistance to prompt variation, calibration, and broad capability retention on public downstream tasks such as MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, Winogrande, TruthfulQA, and perplexity on WikiText-103 or The Pile validation split. Also test sequential edits at increasing batch sizes and measure edit success after delays induced by unrelated prompting, to capture whether apparent success is brittle. Compare against a parameter-free baseline that leaves weights untouched, such as retrieval-augmented generation or an external memory/prompting mechanism backed by a public corpus like Wikipedia or Wikidata-derived passages. If parameter-editing methods maintain high rewrite success while preserving broad task performance and specificity under these realistic evaluations, that weakens the claim; if success drops materially once paraphrases, locality, and capability retention are measured, that supports the claim that near-perfect reported results do not survive realistic evaluation. If the parameter-free baseline matches or exceeds factual update utility with less collateral damage, that also supports the claim’s final conclusion. This experiment would be partly unnecessary if prior work had already released standardized, publicly reproducible evaluations covering these exact broader metrics rather than only narrow rewrite success.

To address subclaim 3, subclaim 4, and subclaim 5, perform a mechanistic geometry study of how localized parameter edits move internal representations and outputs. On a public model and public edit datasets such as CounterFact, compute hidden-state covariance spectra layer by layer on a large public text corpus such as WikiText-103, C4 samples, or The Pile subsets. Then, for each parameter edit produced by methods like ROME or MEMIT, project the induced change in activations and logits onto principal directions of the pre-edit representation space, measuring whether effect size is concentrated in low-variance directions. Next, quantify propagation by tracing changes in token distributions and hidden activations over a broad set of unrelated prompts drawn from public corpora and benchmarks, not just the edited subject neighborhood. Use causal tracing or activation patching to determine whether the edit remains localized or causes system-wide shifts across layers and prompts. As a control, compare to random weight perturbations matched in norm and sparsity, and to edits constrained to align with high-variance directions. If factual edits consistently show stronger amplification along low-variance directions and broader output shifts than matched controls, that supports the claim that the limitation is geometric and that localized edits propagate globally. If instead edits remain confined and amplification is not enriched in low-variance directions, the geometric explanation is weakened. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already public mechanistic evidence directly connecting edit vectors, representation spectra, and broad prompt-level propagation in the same models and settings.

To address subclaim 6, subclaim 7, and subclaim 8, evaluate scaling behavior as many edits accumulate and compare parameter-editing against a parameter-free alternative that explicitly leaves weights unchanged. Using a public model and a large public factual benchmark such as CounterFact plus Wikidata-derived fact triples or zsRE, apply sequential edits in batches ranging from 1 to hundreds or thousands. After each batch, measure rewrite success, preservation of earlier edits, interference between related and unrelated facts, and broad capability retention on public general benchmarks. In parallel, build a parameter-free system using retrieval over a public knowledge source such as Wikipedia passages or a Wikidata-to-text corpus indexed with a standard open retriever, and verify by checksum or direct parameter comparison that model weights remain identical before and after updates. Add the same new facts by updating only the external datastore or prompt memory, then evaluate with the same metrics and latency/cost measurements. If parameter-editing damage grows superlinearly or success degrades as edits accumulate while the parameter-free approach maintains stable core performance with competitive factual update accuracy, that supports both damage compounding and the claim that a parameter-free approach is a serious alternative rather than merely a fallback. If parameter-editing remains stable across many edits and clearly outperforms parameter-free methods without capability loss, that weakens the claim. This experiment would be partly unnecessary if there were already large-scale public longitudinal studies of hundreds or thousands of sequential edits with matched comparisons to weight-unchanged baselines.

To address subclaims 1 and 2, run a realistic head-to-head evaluation of parameter-based editors on public models and factual-edit datasets. Use open-weight models such as GPT-2 XL, GPT-J-6B, or Llama-2-7B if licensing permits, and apply representative editing methods such as fine-tuning, ROME, MEMIT, and MEND on CounterFact and zsRE from HuggingFace. Evaluate not only the original edit prompt, but also paraphrased prompts, reverse/relation-neighbor prompts, multi-hop questions from MQuAKE, unrelated factual probes, WikiText-103 or OpenWebText perplexity, and general capability benchmarks such as HellaSwag, ARC, and MMLU subsets. Compare reported near-perfect edit success under the original benchmark protocol with performance under this broader protocol. If edit success remains high while locality, perplexity, and downstream capability scores remain statistically unchanged, the claim that parameter editing cannot reliably update facts without damage is weakened. If success collapses under paraphrases or unrelated capabilities degrade, that supports the claim that prior near-perfect results do not survive realistic evaluation. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary if prior papers already released full edit logs, model checkpoints, and evaluations on paraphrase, locality, downstream capability, and perplexity metrics across the same public datasets.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, test whether editing damage is geometrically linked to low-variance representation directions and global propagation. For a chosen model and editor from Experiment 1, collect hidden states on a large public corpus such as WikiText-103 or OpenWebText and estimate layerwise covariance spectra using PCA or randomized SVD. After each factual edit from CounterFact or zsRE, measure the induced activation change across layers and prompts, decompose that change into high-variance versus low-variance principal directions, and quantify amplification by the ratio of output-logit or downstream-loss change per unit activation change in each subspace. As a control, inject synthetic perturbations of matched norm into high-variance and low-variance directions without performing factual edits, then compare the effect on unrelated factual probes and language-modeling loss. If real edits and matched synthetic low-variance perturbations cause disproportionately large logit shifts and affect many unrelated prompts or layers, that supports the geometric explanation and the global-propagation subclaim. If edit effects align mainly with high-variance directions or remain confined to edited facts and nearby layers, the geometric explanation is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by direct mechanistic evidence from prior work showing the full eigenspace decomposition of edit-induced representation changes and their causal effects on unrelated behavior.

To address subclaims 6, 7, and 8, evaluate edit accumulation and compare it with a parameter-free alternative. Sequentially apply increasing numbers of edits, for example 1, 10, 100, 1000, and 5000 edits from CounterFact or zsRE, using the strongest parameter-editing method from Experiment 1, and after each batch measure edit success, paraphrase generalization, locality, WikiText-103 perplexity, HellaSwag or ARC accuracy, and unrelated factual QA accuracy. In parallel, implement a parameter-free baseline such as retrieval-augmented generation over an edit memory or in-context editing using the same edited facts; verify that base model weights are untouched by comparing parameter hashes before and after use. Evaluate both systems under the same latency and context-budget constraints, including conflict cases and multi-hop questions from MQuAKE. If parameter-editing damage grows with the number of edits while the parameter-free method preserves base capabilities and achieves competitive edited-fact accuracy, this supports the claim that damage compounds and that parameter-free editing is a serious alternative. If parameter editing scales to thousands of edits without degradation and clearly outperforms the parameter-free method on reliability, cost, and latency, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary if there were already public cumulative-edit checkpoints, edit-order ablations, and comparable retrieval-based baselines evaluated with identical metrics and compute budgets.

To address subclaims 1 and 2, run a preregistered realistic replication of parameter-based editing on open-weight models such as GPT-J-6B and Llama-2-7B using public implementations of ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning. Apply edits from the publicly available CounterFact and zsRE datasets, while separating evaluation prompts from edit prompts and testing held-out paraphrases, multi-hop consequences using RippleEdits, neighborhood facts, unrelated factual queries, and general capabilities using public benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, and TruthfulQA. Compare edited models against the original model and simple prompting controls, reporting confidence intervals across models, methods, relation types, random seeds, and both favorable and adversarial prompt formats. Reliability should require simultaneous edit success, paraphrase generalization, preservation of neighboring and unrelated facts, and no meaningful degradation of general benchmarks—not merely exact recall on the edit prompt. If high success persists across these tests without statistically or practically significant collateral degradation, the claim and the assertion that prior near-perfect results fail realistic evaluation would be weakened; success restricted to benchmark-like prompts or accompanied by capability loss would support them. This experiment could be made largely unnecessary by public, independently reproduced evaluations that release all edited checkpoints, prompts, seeds, and per-example capability results under the same simultaneous criteria.

To address subclaims 3, 4, and 5, test the proposed geometric mechanism by measuring and causally manipulating the alignment of localized weight edits with low-variance representation directions. For each model and edit from CounterFact or zsRE, estimate layerwise activation covariances from a public text corpus such as WikiText-103 or a fixed C4 validation subset, decompose activations into variance eigendirections, and project the editor-induced change in hidden states and weights onto variance quantiles. Measure amplification as the ratio between downstream output or hidden-state change and the original perturbation, both on the edited prompt and on thousands of unrelated corpus prompts; measure global propagation by the fraction and semantic diversity of unrelated prompts whose token distributions, representations, or answers change beyond preregistered thresholds. Then perform a causal intervention: construct norm-matched edits constrained either to low-variance or high-variance subspaces, and separately remove low-variance components from the original edit while matching edit success as closely as possible. Stronger downstream amplification and broader collateral effects for low-variance-aligned edits, plus reduced damage after removing those components, would support a geometric explanation; no relationship after controlling for edit norm, layer, conditioning, and efficacy—or equal effects from high-variance directions—would weaken it and suggest optimization or dataset artifacts instead. Because covariance estimates may be corpus-dependent, repeat with WikiText-103 and C4. The experiment could be avoided if existing work supplied released checkpoints and causal subspace interventions, rather than correlations alone, across several architectures and corpora.

To address subclaims 6, 7, and 8, conduct a sequential-edit comparison between the strongest parameter editor identified in Experiment 1 and a parameter-free external-memory method that retrieves edited subject-relation-object records and inserts them into the prompt without modifying model parameters. Draw randomized edit streams of 1, 10, 100, 500, and 1,000 compatible facts from CounterFact and zsRE, evaluate after every logarithmic checkpoint, and use identical factual, paraphrase, multi-hop, neighborhood, unrelated, and core-capability tests. Verify the parameter-free condition by hashing every model tensor before and after the run; also track retrieval accuracy, context length, latency, memory footprint, edit insertion and deletion cost, conflicts, and robustness to distractor records. Fit degradation-versus-edit-count curves over multiple seeds and test whether capability or locality damage grows superlinearly, linearly, or not at all. Compounding collateral loss for parameter editing would support subclaim 6, while flat damage would weaken it. Identical tensor hashes would establish that the retrieval method leaves weights untouched, although not that it is useful. If external memory matches or exceeds parameter editing on edit accuracy and generalization while preserving capabilities at acceptable compute and latency, it is a serious alternative; poor retrieval, weak multi-hop use, or prohibitive overhead would favor parameter editing despite weight preservation. This experiment could be made unnecessary by public head-to-head sequential-edit studies that release complete edit streams, checkpoints or tensor hashes, retrieval stores, and matched quality-cost measurements.
